Fetal Echo Project · Unit XA5 · Diagnose tier · v0.3

The complete fetal echocardiogram

DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

You will be able to

  • State when a fetal echocardiogram is done and how follow-up is timed.
  • List the views of a complete study and what each must show.
  • Separate required from optional elements for imaging, measurement and Doppler.
  • Say what makes a study complete, and what to report when it is not.

Screening scan and fetal echocardiogram

The Detect units teach the screening scan: five planes on every pregnancy. This unit describes the fetal echocardiogram, the examination that follows a referral.

The guideline endorses limiting the performance and supervision of fetal echocardiograms to appropriately trained or experienced paediatric cardiologists, maternal-fetal medicine specialists, obstetricians or radiologists with fetal echocardiography skills.1

Two-dimensional imaging, colour Doppler and spectral Doppler should all be used, with settings optimised for the fetal heart.2

Timing and follow-up

The optimal window for a comprehensive transabdominal fetal echocardiogram is 18 to 22 weeks.3

A normal mid-trimester fetal echocardiogram generally needs no follow-up, unless there is concern for a progressive lesion. Where one is suspected, repeat assessment is recommended at intervals of up to 2 to 4 weeks.4,5

An abnormal heart is usually reassessed every 2 to 8 weeks until about 34 to 36 weeks, the interval depending on the lesion and the clinical concerns. Near term, reassessment targets findings that could change care immediately after birth.6,7

The follow-up interval should be decided by the fetal cardiology and obstetric teams caring for the patient.8

Start with a survey

In the initial survey, look for fluid around the heart, in the pleural spaces and in the abdomen, and record whether it is present.9

Assign abdominal situs from an upper abdominal cross-section showing the stomach, liver, descending aorta and systemic veins, with careful attention to fetal lie and transducer orientation. Two-dimensional imaging is required for visceral and atrial situs; colour is optional.10,11

Four-chamber view

Examine the heart from at least two orthogonal planes, depending on the size, thickness and orientation of the structure.12

What the guideline requires in and around the four-chamber view.13,14,15,16,17,18,19,20

ElementRequiredOptional
Cardiac axisAssessed on two-dimensional imagingMeasuring the angle
Cardiac sizeMeasured cardiac-to-thoracic area ratio-
Systemic venous connectionsTwo-dimensional and colour imaging-
Pulmonary venous connectionsAt least one vein from each side, two-dimensional and colourFurther veins from either lung
Atrioventricular connectionsTwo-dimensional and colour imaging-
Ventricular septumTwo-dimensional and colour imaging, locating any defect-
VentriclesRelative size assessed on two-dimensional imagingMaximum length and width

Outflow tracts

The normal left ventricular outflow view shows the outflow below the aortic valve, the valve itself, the region above it and the ascending aorta.21

The normal right ventricular outflow view shows the tract below the pulmonary valve, the valve and the proximal pulmonary trunk. The bifurcation may come into this plane.22

The origins of the right and left pulmonary arteries at the bifurcation require two-dimensional and colour imaging. Measuring their diameters is optional.23

Three-vessel views

In the normal three-vessel view the pulmonary trunk, ascending aorta and superior vena cava appear in that order from fetal left to right. Record any abnormality of vessel number, size, alignment or arrangement.24,25

In the normal three-vessel-and-trachea view the two arches join the descending aorta on the left of the trachea. Colour Doppler should show that both arches are patent, and the direction of flow in each.26,27

Aortic and ductal arch sidedness should be documented at every fetal echocardiogram.28

Sagittal views

Bicaval view: establishes whether the inferior vena cava is continuous, and whether the superior and inferior venae cavae lie on the same side.29,30

Aortic arch, long axis: establish continuity from the ascending to the descending aorta, and assess the ascending aorta, transverse arch and isthmus for hypoplasia.31,32

Ductal arch, long axis: a sagittal plane just to the left of the fetal midline usually shows it. To assess ductal restriction, evaluate systolic and diastolic velocities at both the pulmonary and the aortic end, with colour or spectral Doppler or both.33,34

Measuring the ductus and the aortic isthmus is optional in the standard assessment of arch size and shape.35

Short-axis views

A high short-axis view shows the aortic valve face-on, with the right ventricular outflow and pulmonary artery wrapping in front of it.36

A low short-axis view can show muscular ventricular septal defects when colour Doppler is added.37

Measurements

Measurement of the mitral and tricuspid annulus in early diastole is required. Measurement of the aortic and pulmonary valve annuli is also required.38,39

The guideline is not consistent on when in the cycle the aortic and pulmonary annuli are measured: its text and a table footnote specify systole, while the table row allows end-diastole or early systole. This course does not yet teach one reading as the rule.39

Pulsed-wave Doppler

The guideline's table lists as required: umbilical vein, ductus venosus, at least one pulmonary vein on each side, tricuspid and mitral inflow, aortic and pulmonary outflow, the distal ductus arteriosus and the umbilical artery.40

The table marks as optional: hepatic vein, the venae cavae, branch pulmonary arteries, middle cerebral artery, a combined left ventricular inflow and outflow recording, and tissue Doppler at the lateral annulus. Whether the aortic arch and isthmus are required or optional is not settled within the guideline.41

Rhythm and function

Every fetal echocardiogram must document heart rate and rhythm, and must include a qualitative assessment of systolic and diastolic function.42,43

When findings raise concern about cardiac function or output, a quantitative assessment should be performed. When dysfunction is suspected, it is important at initial imaging to assess for fetal hydrops or its component findings.44,45

Regurgitation through an atrioventricular valve on Doppler may indicate systolic dysfunction.46

When is the study complete?

If a standard view cannot be obtained, the study is complete only if all the cardiovascular structures have been adequately seen by another approach, or are anatomically absent.47

If the study remains non-diagnostic after optimisation, the report should state the limitations.48

The study should include still images, moving clips and a structured report.49

Complete fetal echocardiogram: views

  • Survey for fluid around the heart, in the pleural spaces and in the abdomen9
  • Abdominal situs: stomach, liver, descending aorta, systemic veins10
  • Heart examined from at least two orthogonal planes; axis; cardiac-to-thoracic area ratio12,13,14
  • Systemic and pulmonary venous connections, two-dimensional and colour (at least one pulmonary vein each side)15,16
  • Atrioventricular connections and ventricular septum, two-dimensional and colour18,19
  • Left and right outflow tracts; branch pulmonary artery origins21,22,23
  • Three-vessel view; three-vessel-and-trachea view with colour; side of each arch documented25,27,28
  • Bicaval, aortic arch and ductal arch sagittal views29,31,33
  • Short-axis views36,37
  • Four valve annuli measured38,39
  • Pulsed-wave Doppler at the required sites40
  • Rate, rhythm and qualitative function documented42,43
  • Stills, clips and structured report; limitations stated if any49,48
